metadata.title: Groups, Elections, and Overlapping Percentages
metadata.description: Interpret percentage shares in groups, account for intersections, and distinguish turnout from valid-vote bases.
metadata.teachingApproach: Build the model step by step, explain why each operation matches the wording, show intermediate arithmetic, check units and magnitude, then practice transfer with specific remedial feedback.
metadata.sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 11 “Percentage,” printed pages 308–345. Approved scope: Handle voter turnout, invalid votes, candidate shares, winning margins, demographic/group percentages, and nested eligible/participating groups. Teach the inclusion-exclusion relationship for two overlapping categories: percent in either = percent in A + percent in B − percent in both, with complements used for neither or passed-all cases. Translate sequential filters (eligible, turnout, valid votes, candidate share) as successive multipliers. Distinguish percent of votes cast from percent of registered voters and use a consistent total/base in every stage.

content.text: Groups, Elections, and Overlapping Percentages: Interpret percentage shares in groups, account for intersections, and distinguish turnout from valid-vote bases. This lesson builds the method from its meaning, works through the reasoning and checks, then practices it with targeted feedback.

A group percentage is count divided by the stated group total. If 240 of 600 voters support a candidate, the support is 240/600=40%. The total eligible voters and actual voters are different possible bases.

In elections, turnout is votes cast divided by registered voters. Candidate share may instead be votes received divided by valid votes. State which denominator the wording specifies before calculating.
If a fraction of cast ballots is invalid, valid votes are the complement. With 8% invalid out of 25,000 ballots, valid votes are 92%×25,000=23,000.
For a two-candidate election with no other valid choices, the candidate counts sum to valid votes. If one candidate receives p% of valid votes, the other gets (100−p)% of valid votes.
A winning margin is the difference in vote counts, not one candidate’s percentage alone. If a candidate gets 54% of 40,000 valid votes, the opponent gets 46%; margin is 8%×40,000=3,200.
If turnout and invalid rates are both given, apply them in sequence. For 80,000 registered voters, 75% turnout, and 4% invalid ballots, valid votes=80,000×0.75×0.96=57,600.
For overlapping groups, inclusion-exclusion prevents double counting: number in A or B = A+B−both. Subtract the overlap once because it was counted in both group totals.
If every person in a population belongs to at least one of two groups, neither group = total−(A+B−both). Check that all quantities refer to the same population.

With three sets, add the three single-set totals, subtract pairwise overlaps, then add the triple overlap once. The triple intersection was subtracted three times, so adding it once restores one count.
A “neither” or “exactly one” question needs careful set logic. Exactly one of A and B equals A-only plus B-only, or A+B−2(both).

When group membership is reported in percentages, convert each percentage to a count on the shared total before applying inclusion-exclusion. This works only if all rates use the same total population.
A count can be recovered from its percentage if the base is known: count=p%×total. Conversely, if count and rate are known, total=count/(p/100).
Percentages from different bases should not be added. A turnout percent uses registered voters; a vote share uses valid votes. Convert both to counts first if they need to be combined.
Sanity checks: an intersection cannot exceed either set; a union cannot exceed the whole population; valid votes cannot exceed ballots cast; votes for candidates cannot exceed valid votes.
Draw a two-circle diagram or a short table for each problem. Label the overlap explicitly, then compute “at least one,” “neither,” or “exactly one” from the diagram.
